title: Challenges in translating mesenchymal stem cell therapies for trauma and critical care
abstract: Traumatic injuries demand immediate hemorrhage control and resuscitation, as well as definitive repair and infection management to prevent death from hemorrhagic shock.1-3 Recent advances in hemorrhage control and blood-based, hemostatic resuscitation can reduce the risk of early death due to bleeding, but a significant burden of morbidity and mortality thought to be caused by inflammation leading to multiorgan failure (MOF) persists and, currently, adequate treatment modalities are lacking. Stem cells, which include embryonic stem cells (ES cells), induced pluripotent stem cells (iPS cells), and mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) are unspecialized, multipotent progenitor cells with the capability of self-renewal followed by differentiation.4-15 They respond to inflammatory mediators and home to the site of injury and can release paracrine factors for growth signaling and immunomodulation.16, 17 By utilizing these mechanisms, stem cells may reduce mortality due to MOF and promote wound healing. Stem cells have been shown to hold great promise in treating other pathophysiologic states in which inflammation plays a major role such as acute graft-versus-host disease, acute respiratory distress syndrome, myocardial infarction, and stroke.18-23 Thus, cellular therapy with stem cells for traumatic injuries also holds great promise. However, a major limitation to the use of either ES or iPS cells has been the formation of teratomas.24-28 MSCs are adult stem cells generally harvested from marrow, but also found in the stromal vascular fraction of other tissues.29-32 Upon appropriate signaling, MSCs differentiate into bone, cartilage, or fat cells.33-35 Additionally, they appear to have a paracrine function and have also been termed mesenchymal signaling cells or mesenchymal stromal cells.36-42 While MSCs have been shown to home to tumors, unlike ES or iPS cells, MSCs do not form teratomas.43-45 The therapeutic potential of MSCs rests upon their regenerative capabilities, medicinal anti-inflammatory properties, and improved safety profile over other stem cells.46, 47 In considering the potential use of MSCs in the early management of civilian or military trauma, an understanding of the pathophysiologic context of their use is required. For both civilians and military personnel, hemorrhage is the leading potentially reversible cause of traumatic death.48 In the last two conflicts in Southwest Asia, 26% of 4090 "killed in action" deaths were deemed potentially survivable. Fully 92% of these, or 984 deaths, were due to hemorrhage.49 Deaths due to hemorrhage are due to anatomic disruption and coagulopathy. In Kandahar, Afghanistan, 1.5% of the admissions were multiamputees; they required initiation of massive transfusion protocols with a mean of 54 units of blood products. Overall, in the last two conflicts of Operation Iraqi Freedom and Operation Enduring Freedom 13.6% of patients received transfusions. Coagulopathy, as evidenced by a mean international normalized ratio of more than 1.5 in patients receiving a transfusion, correlated with a fivefold increase in mortality.50, 51 In severe trauma complicated by coagulopathy, there is massive fibrinogen consumption, with altered clotting kinetics and fibrinolysis, as well as platelet (PLT) consumption and dysfunction. Crystalloid fluid administration causes hemodilution and acidosis, and frequently hypothermia, adding iatrogenic injury that worsens bleeding. Decreased tissue perfusion with blood loss leads to tissue anoxia and acidosis. This completes the lethal triad of acidosis, hypothermia and coagulopathy.52-55 The breach of the endothelium with tissue disruption leads to exposure of tissue factor (TF) and activation of the coagulation pathway as well as suppression of endothelial cell function. Nitric oxide metabolism is disrupted with decreased expression of endothelial nitric oxide synthase and thus decreased synthesis of nitric oxide, increased PLT, and neutrophil adhesion results. With lengthy hemorrhagic shock, tissues begin to express inducible nitric oxide synthase leading to a profound hypotension.56 The endothelial disruption also leads to loss of local anti-inflammatory properties and induction of fibrinolysis. How will MSCs be used in the early management of trauma? As immunomodulatory cells, it has been proposed that systemically administered MSCs may reduce the risk of multiorgan failure. The question is whether acute use of MSCs would alleviate or potentially exacerbate acute traumatic coagulopathy and how they will affect the risk of postresuscitation thrombosis, a leading cause of trauma-related morbidity and mortality. How this envisaged use of MSCs will influence wound healing, which is thought to require MSC homing to damaged tissues where they play an innate immune as well as trophic role during tissue remodeling remains to be determined. Systemic administration of MSCs would require placing multifunctional cells into a highly perturbed physiologic setting undergoing complex clinical interventions. MSCs have been isolated from multiple organs in addition to marrow, including heart, liver, kidney, umbilical cord blood, and adipose tissue.29-31 They are not isolated as a pure cell type but are a minute population selected from the total cell population. Within the marrow, MSCs differ in phenotype depending on their niche. Endosteal MSCs supply hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) quiescence factors, while perivascular MSCs, at some distance from the endosteum, supply factors stimulating HSC activation and differentiation.57 Consider also that endothelial cells usually separate MSCs from blood, which begs the question of how compatible MSCs are with blood. MSCs are known to express TF.58, 59 Phosphatidylserine (PS) is exposed during trypsin release from tissue culture plastic or during the recovery from frozen storage. Primary MSC products contain contaminating cells and other biomaterial including microvesicles. TF, PS surface expression, and microvesicles are all procoagulant.60, 61 What are the effects of MSC expansion on these variables and what are the potential interactions with the recipient, particularly in the setting of severe trauma? It is possible that MSCs will behave as beneficial hemostatic agents, or they could produce an excessively procoagulant environment, depending on dose and timing, and require concomitant anticoagulant administration to prevent venous thromboembolism or disseminated coagulopathy. Stephenne and colleagues62 found that MSCs accelerated clotting due to increased TF expression. When using human adult liver progenitor cells, a type of MSC isolated from liver, they were able to limit thrombotic events by coinfusion of bivalirudin and unfractionated heparin. Such an approach would not be feasible in a still-coagulopathic trauma patient that may require further operative interventions. TF expression has been found to be up regulated by multiple agents including IL-1α, TGF-β. CD40, VEGF, LPS, hypoxia, and shear stress.61 NF-κB has been found to play a critical role in regulation of TF expression.63 MSCs infused after trauma will encounter an environment containing elevated levels of these factors. While MSC anti-inflammatory effects may reduce the expression of these factors, it is also possible that the MSC phenotype will be rendered more procoagulant by the host. Thus, in addition to determining how collection, expansion, and processing of MSCs may contribute to potential infusional toxicities, it will be important to study cell–host interactions to understand the safety and efficacy variables of this cell therapy product. As might be expected, there are myriad complexities in MSC–blood interactions. In addition to expressing the procoagulant compounds TF and PS on their surfaces, MSCs also can express the anticoagulant TF pathway inhibitor and fibrinolytics such as tissue plasminogen activator and urokinase plasminogen activator and its receptor.58 MSCs also express the antifibrinolytic, plasminogen activator inhibitor.65, 66 MSCs express long pentraxin 3 (PTX3), an acute-phase multimeric glycoprotein. PTX3 is involved in inflammation, innate immunity, extracellular matrix deposition, and wound healing through potentiation of fibrinolysis.67, 68 In an acidic environment, PTX3 accelerates fibrinolysis by enhancing plasminogen and fibrin binding. However, persistently high levels of PTX3 during sepsis are associated with worse outcomes. It is unknown how the expression of all these critical factors in coagulation and fibrinolysis varies across the different MSC sources, it is unknown how culture conditions affect them, and it is unknown what effects dosage or route of administration may have. Moll and colleagues64 found fibronectin 1, collagen type 1, and TF surface expression on MSCs significantly increased at Passage 6 versus Passage 3. Although they observed profound donor variability, in an in vitro measure of instant blood-mediated coagulation and inflammatory response, at 15,000 MSCs/mL, free PLTs were reduced approximately 50% at 30 minutes for all donors. This PLT activation was MSC dose and time dependent. The coagulation cascade was initiated—both visible clots were seen and the levels of thrombin–anti-thrombin complexes increased, again in a dose- and time-dependent manner. Tellingly, PLT activation and elevated thrombin–anti-thrombin complexes complexes were dependent on cell passage; later-passage MSCs were more procoagulant. The consequences of these MSC phenotypic changes for the trauma patient are anything but clear: addition of MSCs could exacerbate or resolve coagulopathy and PLT dysfunction; it could result in enhanced fibrinolysis and, thus, enhanced wound healing, but possibly cause late rebleeding. The question of MSC compatibility with stored blood products and hemostatic adjuncts is also relevant for the trauma patient. Should timing and route of administration be different for MSCs and other resuscitation products? Consider the increased use of tranexamic acid (TXA) to control bleeding in trauma since the publication of the CRASH-2 trial.69 Widely used TXA protocols call for delivery to the patient within 3 hours. Within this time frame, TXA demonstrated a reduced odds ratio (OR) for mortality. However, given after 3 hours from injury, TXA was associated with an increased OR for mortality. Timing of administration is critical for this antifibrinolytic.70 Will similar considerations hold for MSCs in trauma? Route of delivery of MSCs represents another important consideration in optimizing this therapy. Wounds are often poorly perfused and hypoxic. Hypoxia increases the MSC microvesicle concentrations of UPAR, VEGF, and IL-6 and other cytokines and trophic factors. In situations such as traumatic brain injury where the injury core is surrounded by a less-damaged perilesional area, which is more receptive to treatment, direct injection of MSCs into the hypoxic wound may be a more effective route than IV delivery. Studies are required to optimize the possible combination of local versus systemic administration and frequency of dosing. Feasibility of such treatments and costs will also need to be evaluated.71, 72 The immunomodulatory properties of MSCs and their potential capacity to reduce the risk of MOF should be studied in relation to the observed capacity of stored blood products to cause immunosuppression or transfusion-related immunomodulation.73, 74 If MSCs are given during a massive transfusion protocol with multiple blood products, would there be additive effects? It would be helpful to have biomarkers to differentiate "good" immunomodulation from "bad" transfusion-related immunomodulation. If MSCs are shown to be beneficial for the trauma patient, what would be the transfusion trigger? Could vital signs, such as heart rate, systolic blood pressure, shock index, or lactate measurement guide the decision?74 What endpoint is targeted? How will the need for redosing be determined? Should MSCs be integrated into a point-of-injury protocol for tactical damage control resuscitation or given in the ICU or much later during reconstruction and rehabilitation?75 Clearly, it would be helpful to have biomarkers for MSC safety and efficacy to rationally design treatment algorithms. While responding to the challenges outlined above, the field of cellular therapy is also undergoing an organizational evolution. One model for the field's development is patterned on the pharmaceutical industry, in which highly characterized, perhaps uniform or genetically modified MSCs will be produced for off-the-shelf use. Another model is the "blood banking" model in which allogeneic or autologous MSCs from many donors are expanded and stored with minimal modification or characterization across many organizations. Finally, there is the "clinical" model, in which autologous mixed MSC and mononuclear cell populations are reapplied to the patient locally or systemically with minimal manipulation. Each of these models presents certain advantages and disadvantages. Clearly, the "pharma" model offers the highest degree of controls on product characteristics and comparability across clinical trials, but is likely to result in constrained supplies and high costs. The blood bank model offers broader availability and cost advantages at the price of product variability. The clinical model reduces risks associated with allogeneic products, but may be very limited in its practicability and perhaps efficacy due the complexities of ensuring timely and adequate collections to allow proper dosing and timing in critically ill patients. Which development model is most appropriate? Can we identify potency markers for MSCs that allow us to define an envelope of acceptable performance that facilitates simultaneous product development along all three pathways? Current investigational metrics examine tropism, endothelial permeability, cytokine release, and synthesis of the extracellular matrix. Are these reliable and appropriate biomarkers of MSC efficacy in trauma or do we need additional functional correlates such as alterations in T-cell activation or macrophage polarization? Ideally, positive outcomes should correlate with known biomarkers. This will require further preclinical testing of MSCs, but the payoff will be more rational clinical trial design and improved comparability between clinical trials. Adopting broadly accepted standards for MSC evaluation will greatly facilitate growth in this branch of cellular therapy. In summary, application of MSCs in the setting of trauma and coagulopathy presents unique opportunities and challenges that have received comparatively little attention to date. The field of MSC therapy lacks adequate potency and safety biomarkers generally, but certainly none have been rigorously validated in complex, critically ill patients receiving significant quantities of stored blood products, hemostatic adjuncts, and other interventions that alter the coagulation and inflammation host environment so dramatically. MSCs have not even been adequately studied in relevant animal models to guide clinical development. Questions that require urgent attention include source of cells (marrow, other?), mechanism of action, selection of patients, dose, route of delivery (IV, IO, other?), timing, preclinical efficacy testing, clinical biomarkers of potency, endpoint selection, and integration with other blood products and hemostatic adjuncts. These challenges are not insurmountable and while one does not want "perfect" to be the enemy of "good," a robust investment in defining acceptable performance metrics is the catalyst that will spur the development of the field. The authors have disclosed no conflicts of interest.

title: Conditions of Living
abstract: Conditions of Living examines the rise of economic segregation in recent housing developments, a phenomenon commonly known as ‘poor doors’. This socially engaged artwork by Anthony Luvera was created in collaboration with a community forum of local residents living in Tower Hamlets and draws upon extensive research into the social, political, and economic evolution of market-driven ‘affordable’ housing provision, and the state of social housing today. Brought together from almost 1,000 households in eight developments, participants in the Conditions of Living Community Forum have a range of housing tenure backgrounds, from social and affordable rental accommodation to shared and sole ownership. Using photography, sound recordings, and discussion-based activities facilitated to enable participants to share their personal experiences of living in these developments, Luvera worked with the Community Forum to consider how economic segregation in housing operates, and how restrictions expand outward from separate entrances to access to amenities, resources, and public space. Through group workshops and individual meetings, participants were invited to explore issues relating to why some buildings have segregated entrances, and how architecture and planning affect access to key social rights such as healthcare, culture, the environment, education, and transport. Segregation in housing developments can occur in a variety of ways, through physical doors leading to different parts of the building; separate floors assigned to non-market rate flats or the so-called affordable housing units; distinct internal segments of the same building usually with isolated lifts; entire blocks within a wider complex; or specific amenities that are restricted to certain residents based on the type of unit they live in. Local authorities allow property developers to design ‘poor doors’ into their housing developments and consequently embed segregation therein. London is one of the world’s last major cities yet to ban ‘poor doors’ despite years of political proclamations against this segregationist practice. The built environment plays a powerful role in determining the ways people live together and is at the core of the experience of housing. Architecture and planning can be used to enforce social inequalities through the privileging of market forces, resulting in discrimination and segregation. Conditions of Living brings together research and the experiences of those living in the buildings to construct an image of this much discussed, yet often invisible phenomenon. Conditions of Living invites us to reflect on these convoluted systems and contemplate alternative possibilities for housing conditions, communal living, and collective action. Conditions of Living was first exhibited in Conditions of Living: Home and Homelessness in London's East End at Four Corners, curated by Carla Mitchell and Eleni Parousi with Anthony Luvera from 30 June 2023 to 2 September 2023. The exhibition was accompanied by an extensive public engagement programme, including the following events: Thurs 13 July, 7pm. Curator's talk. Sat 15 July, 11.30 – 2pm. Public and social housing in the East End from the late 19th century, walk with Mike Berlin (Birkbeck, University of London). Tues 18 July, 6.30 – 7.30pm. Artist talk with Anthony Luvera. Thurs 27 July, 6.30 – 8pm. From the Nichol to the Boundary: how London’s first planned council estate came to be built, talk by Sarah Wise. Thurs 31 Aug, 6.30pm – 8pm. Struggles for better housing and the Stepney Rent Strikes 1937-39, talk by David Rosenberg followed by screening of short films. Fri 1 Sept, 10.30 - 1pm. Conditions of Living: long table discussion. This event brought together speakers engaged in issues surrounding housing precarity, economic segregation, market-driven ‘affordable’ homes and social housing today, including Anthony Luvera, Hannah Caller (Focus E15), Mel Nowicki (Oxford Brookes University), Pablo Sendra (The Bartlett School of Planning, University College London), Suz Muna (Social Housing Action Campaign), and Paul Watt (London School of Economics and Political Science). In 2025, Conditions of Living was realised as a co-created publication amplifying the lived experiences of residents in economically segregated housing. Developed through the Conditions of Living Community Forum, the publication enabled participants to shape how their stories are told, not as subjects, but as agents of change. Participants reported personal benefits including improved wellbeing, digital and creative skill development, and a deeper sense of social connection and pride in contributing to a policy-facing publication. Resident’s voices were interweaved with leading thinkers on the issue: Simon Hill (New Economics Foundation), Mel Nowicki (Oxford Brookes), Paul Watt (LSE), Suzanne Muna (SHAC), and Samir Jeraj (New Statesman). The publication was widely disseminated to policymakers, housing providers, and campaigners across the United Kingdom and internationally. In July 2025, Conditions of Living was shortlisted for the 2025 Photo-Text Book Award at the Rencontres d'Arles Photography Festival. In the field of practice-led research, Conditions of Living has been characterised as an innovative model of socially engaged photography, capable of contributing to real-world change.

title: Trust-Aware Sequential Decision Making and Rollout Planning for Resilient Multi-Robot Systems
abstract: Sequential decision-making in multi-robot systems typically assumes that planning information is reliable and that agents execute the actions anticipated by the planner. Compromised agents can violate both assumptions, creating a mismatch between the planning model and physical execution. We study this problem in online multi-robot routing under localization spoofing. We introduce a distance-constrained spoofing model for monitor-aware adversaries, together with a tiered bipartite matching strategy that maximizes assignment influence while limiting spoofing magnitude. To mitigate such attacks, we develop a trust-aware monitor that combines probabilistic localization trust, calibrated using real GPS spoofing data, with behavioral evidence from task execution to classify agents and remove detected adversaries from subsequent planning. We further show that undetected adversaries can cause rollout to lose its expected cost-improvement behavior by violating planner-execution consistency. Trust-aware removal restores this consistency after detection, enabling stable routing and recovery of rollout's empirical advantage over the base policy. Experiments using real GPS spoofing datasets and San Francisco taxicab demand demonstrate effective detection and resilient routing across varying spoofing capabilities, adversarial fleet sizes, adaptive attacks, monitoring configurations, and rollout horizons.

title: Causal Policy Gradient for Whole-Body Mobile Manipulation
abstract: Developing the next generation of household robot helpers requires combining locomotion and interaction capabilities, which is generally referred to as mobile manipulation (MoMa). MoMa tasks are difficult due to the large action space of the robot and the common multi-objective nature of the task, e.g., efficiently reaching a goal while avoiding obstacles. Current approaches often segregate tasks into navigation without manipulation and stationary manipulation without locomotion by manually matching parts of the action space to MoMa sub-objectives (e.g. learning base actions for locomotion objectives and learning arm actions for manipulation). This solution prevents simultaneous combinations of locomotion and interaction degrees of freedom and requires human domain knowledge for both partitioning the action space and matching the action parts to the sub-objectives. In this paper, we introduce Causal MoMa, a new reinforcement learning framework to train policies for typical MoMa tasks that makes use of the most favorable subspace of the robot's action space to address each sub-objective. Causal MoMa automatically discovers the causal dependencies between actions and terms of the reward function and exploits these dependencies through causal policy gradient that reduces gradient variance compared to previous state-of-the-art reinforcement learning algorithms, improving convergence and results. We evaluate the performance of Causal MoMa on three types of simulated robots across different MoMa tasks and demonstrate success in transferring the policies trained in simulation directly to a real robot, where our agent is able to follow moving goals and react to dynamic obstacles while simultaneously and synergistically controlling the whole-body: base, arm, and head. More information at https://sites.google.com/view/causal-moma.

title: TC-Driver: Trajectory Conditioned Driving for Robust Autonomous Racing -- A Reinforcement Learning Approach
abstract: Autonomous racing is becoming popular for academic and industry researchers as a test for general autonomous driving by pushing perception, planning, and control algorithms to their limits. While traditional control methods such as MPC are capable of generating an optimal control sequence at the edge of the vehicles physical controllability, these methods are sensitive to the accuracy of the modeling parameters. This paper presents TC-Driver, a RL approach for robust control in autonomous racing. In particular, the TC-Driver agent is conditioned by a trajectory generated by any arbitrary traditional high-level planner. The proposed TC-Driver addresses the tire parameter modeling inaccuracies by exploiting the heuristic nature of RL while leveraging the reliability of traditional planning methods in a hierarchical control structure. We train the agent under varying tire conditions, allowing it to generalize to different model parameters, aiming to increase the racing capabilities of the system in practice. The proposed RL method outperforms a non-learning-based MPC with a 2.7 lower crash ratio in a model mismatch setting, underlining robustness to parameter discrepancies. In addition, the average RL inference duration is 0.25 ms compared to the average MPC solving time of 11.5 ms, yielding a nearly 40-fold speedup, allowing for complex control deployment in computationally constrained devices. Lastly, we show that the frequently utilized end-to-end RL architecture, as a control policy directly learned from sensory input, is not well suited to model mismatch robustness nor track generalization. Our realistic simulations show that TC-Driver achieves a 6.7 and 3-fold lower crash ratio under model mismatch and track generalization settings, while simultaneously achieving lower lap times than an end-to-end approach, demonstrating the viability of TC-driver to robust autonomous racing.

title: Reciprocal Reward Influence Encourages Cooperation From Self-Interested Agents
abstract: Cooperation between self-interested individuals is a widespread phenomenon in the natural world, but remains elusive in interactions between artificially intelligent agents. Instead, naive reinforcement learning algorithms typically converge to Pareto-dominated outcomes in even the simplest of social dilemmas. An emerging literature on opponent shaping has demonstrated the ability to reach prosocial outcomes by influencing the learning of other agents. However, such methods differentiate through the learning step of other agents or optimize for meta-game dynamics, which rely on privileged access to opponents' learning algorithms or exponential sample complexity, respectively. To provide a learning rule-agnostic and sample-efficient alternative, we introduce Reciprocators, reinforcement learning agents which are intrinsically motivated to reciprocate the influence of opponents' actions on their returns. This approach seeks to modify other agents' $Q$-values by increasing their return following beneficial actions (with respect to the Reciprocator) and decreasing it after detrimental actions, guiding them towards mutually beneficial actions without directly differentiating through a model of their policy. We show that Reciprocators can be used to promote cooperation in temporally extended social dilemmas during simultaneous learning. Our code is available at https://github.com/johnlyzhou/reciprocator/.

title: Can Compact Language Models Search Like Agents? Distillation-Guided Policy Optimization for Preserving Agentic RAG Capabilities
abstract: Reinforcement Learning has emerged as a dominant post-training approach to elicit agentic RAG behaviors such as search and planning from language models. Despite its success with larger models, applying RL to compact models (e.g., 0.5--1B parameters) presents unique challenges. The compact models exhibit poor initial performance, resulting in sparse rewards and unstable training. To overcome these difficulties, we propose Distillation-Guided Policy Optimization (DGPO), which employs cold-start initialization from teacher demonstrations and continuous teacher guidance during policy optimization. To understand how compact models preserve agentic behavior, we introduce Agentic RAG Capabilities (ARC), a fine-grained metric analyzing reasoning, search coordination, and response synthesis. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that DGPO enables compact models to achieve sophisticated agentic search behaviors, even outperforming the larger teacher model in some cases. DGPO makes agentic RAG feasible in computing resource-constrained environments.

title: The Role of Education in Shaping Social and Cultural Identity
abstract: Abstract Education serves as a foundational socialization agent, functioning simultaneously as a transmitter of cultural heritage and a critical catalyst for social evolution. This paper examines the intricate, recursive interplay between formal educational systems and the formation of both individual and collective identity. Through a comprehensive multidisciplinary analysis, it explores how curriculum design, teacher-student power dynamics, and the institutional culture of the school environment influence a learner’s perception of self, group belonging, and civic responsibility. The findings suggest that while education can foster national cohesion and cultural literacy, it frequently functions as a mechanism of exclusion for minority identities if pedagogical practices remain rigid or assimilationist. By synthesizing Social Identity Theory, Critical Pedagogy, and Bourdieu’s notions of cultural capital, this study highlights the urgent necessity for culturally responsive and pluralistic pedagogy in increasingly globalized societies. The article concludes by arguing that educational institutions must transition from engines of state-driven assimilation to platforms of pluralistic empowerment, where identity is treated as a fluid, dynamic, and multifaceted project. Keywords: Social Identity, Cultural Identity, Educational Policy, Socialization, Culturally Responsive Pedagogy, Critical Pedagogy, Inclusive Education, Bourdieu, Cultural Capital. 1. Introduction Education is rarely a neutral enterprise; it acts as both a mirror reflecting societal values and a laboratory for constructing future identities. As individuals navigate the formal pathways of schooling, they engage in a recursive process of internalizing cultural norms, linguistic registers, and social expectations. The institution of the school is, in effect, a microcosm of the state, exerting significant pressure on students to adopt specific worldviews while implicitly or sometimes explicitly others that fall outside the "ideal" citizen profile. The construction of identity within the classroom is not merely an incidental outcome of schooling; it is a foundational, if often obscured, objective of modern state-building. Historically, the advent of universal, compulsory schooling was designed to cultivate "ideal citizens"individuals who subscribe to a shared national narrative, often at the expense of regional, linguistic, or ethnic distinctiveness. This article investigates the systemic mechanisms both visible and invisible through which schools construct and constrain these identities. By examining the tension between nationalistic curricular agendas and the lived realities of increasingly diverse student populations, we can better understand how educational policy dictates the boundaries of belonging, exclusion, and democratic participation. As societies become more interconnected through digital technology and global migration, the role of education in navigating these complexities has never been more critical. We must look beyond simple academic attainment to understand how the school experience molds the architecture of the self, transforming the learner from a passive vessel into an agent of their own cultural synthesis. This study provides a deep dive into the psychological and sociological dimensions of this process, advocating for a pedagogical shift toward empowerment and plurality. 2. Theoretical Framework: The Anatomy of Identity in Education Social Identity Theory, pioneered by Henri Tajfel, posits that an individual’s sense of self is derived, in large part, from group membership. Educational environments categorize students, influencing their self-concept through two primary, interlocking vectors: The Formal Curriculum: This represents the "canon" of knowledge deemed valuable by the state. It dictates whose history is taught, whose literature is celebrated, and which scientific paradigms are validated. When this curriculum is narrow, students from non-dominant groups often perceive a painful disconnect between their home identity and the "official" identity promoted by the state, leading to a state of "double consciousness" described by W.E.B. Du Bois. This disconnect creates a cognitive barrier that can impede learning, as students must constantly mediate between the requirements of the school and the cultural authenticity of their home life. The Hidden Curriculum: Beyond the written textbooks, schools transmit values through unspoken norms, teacher expectations, and social behaviors. This "hidden curriculum" teaches students their place in the social hierarchy, reinforcing gender roles, class expectations, and ethnic prestige through the regulation of dress codes, disciplinary policies, and the physical architecture of classrooms. The subtle messages conveyed by who is praised, who is disciplined, and what is considered "proper" behavior collectively shape the student's internal map of their own social viability. Furthermore, we must integrate Pierre Bourdieu’s concept of "cultural capital." Educational systems tend to reward the cultural capital of the dominant classsuch as mastery of standard linguistic registers and familiarity with bourgeois cultural referencesplacing those from marginalized backgrounds at a distinct structural disadvantage. This necessitates an inquiry into how schools can transition from reinforcing existing inequities to dismantling them through critical pedagogy. As Paulo Freire argued, education must move away from the "banking model" of rote memorization, where students are passive vessels, toward a problem-posing methodology that validates the student’s lived experience as legitimate knowledge. By situating the classroom as a field of struggle, educators can help students decode the systemic forces that shape their identities, thereby fostering agency rather than resignation. The goal is to move toward a model of "transformative education" that views student identity as a site of potentiality rather than a deficit to be corrected. 3. The Psychology of Linguistic Displacement In many post-colonial and multicultural nations, the medium of instruction often conflicts with the learner’s home language, leading to profound identity friction. Research indicates that when schools privilege colonial or dominant languages at the expense of indigenous or heritage tongues, students frequently experience "linguistic alienation." 3.1 The Process of Alienation When a student’s primary tool for communicationtheir mother tongueis excluded from the academic environment, they are effectively told that their home culture lacks academic legitimacy. This leads to a fragmented cultural identity where the student feels compelled to perform a "school persona" that is divorced from their domestic life, often resulting in lower academic self-esteem and cultural estrangement. The school, in this scenario, functions as a site of symbolic violence, where the student's background is not merely ignored but actively invalidated. This alienation is compounded by the psychological toll of being forced to choose between linguistic assimilation and academic success, a choice that fundamentally fractures the self-concept. 3.2 Case Study: The Kura Kaupapa Māori Experience The success of bilingual integration is exemplified by initiatives such as the Kura Kaupapa Māori in New Zealand. By teaching through the medium of the indigenous language and embedding traditional Māori cultural practices into the daily curriculum, these schools demonstrate significant benefits in student outcomes. Research confirms that preserving heritage language is essential not just for cultural survival, but for stable psychological development. These programs illustrate that allowing the "home voice" to coexist with the "school voice" creates a bridge, enabling students to traverse multiple cultural worlds with confidence rather than conflict. By centering Te Aho Matua (the foundational philosophy of these schools), educators have successfully demonstrated that cultural grounding is a prerequisite for, not an obstacle to, academic achievement. This model provides a blueprint for global efforts to reclaim linguistic sovereignty within the classroom. 4. Discussion: Navigating the Globalized Challenge The contemporary challenge for educators is to balance the need for a shared national identityoften required for civic cohesion with the necessity of preserving diverse cultural backgrounds. Globalization has introduced new dimensions to this debate; students now navigate hybrid identities in a digital landscape that is both local and transnational. Additive Bilingualism: Policies that encourage proficiency in both the national/global language and the mother tongue yield the most stable identity outcomes. This prevents the "subtractive" effect where academic gain comes at the cost of cultural loss. Representational Narratives: Historical curricula must move beyond "single stories." When students see their communities reflected accurately in history and literature, their civic participation increases. This requires not just tokenistic inclusions but a systemic shift in how we narrate the nation’s history to include subaltern voices. title: Dreamer: An innovative bone filler paste for the treatment of periodontitis
abstract: Event Abstract Back to Event Dreamer: An innovative bone filler paste for the treatment of periodontitis Giorgio Iviglia1, Clara Cassinelli1, Elisa Torre1 and Marco Morra1 1 Nobil Bio Ricerche srl, R&D, Italy Introduction: Periodontitis is a bacterially induced chronic inflammatory disease that destroys the connective tissue and bone that support teeth. It is nowadays recognized that uncontrolled inflammatory response of cells from the host defense system to oral bacteria, mostly based on genetic predisposition, is at the basis of periodontal tissue loss. Combines the classic properties of mechanical support and biological stimulation with an anti-inflammatory and an anti–osteoclastogenesis effects it is the desiderable goal. Polyphenols, present in grape, wine and winery by-products, are since long known for their anti-inflammatory properties and literature suggests they also stimulate bone regeneration. We developed an innovative paste for bone regeneration in periodontal patients (Dreamer paste) by the exploitation of polyphenol molecules extracted from winery by-products, as anti-inflammatory molecules, mixed with ceramic particles and collagen type I. Materials and Methods: All chemicals used were purchased from Sigma - Aldirich. Collagen type I e was purchased from Sewon Cellontech Ltd. Ceramic particles was prepared mixing HA/ β-TCP (25:75 % wt.) with a porogen agent, and then sintered in disk of 15 mm and ground, to obtain particles from 200 - 300 um. Polyphenols extract were prepared from winery by-products, using Aceton:Water solution with TIMATIC automatic extractor, in a concetration of 1,5 mg/ml. Ceramic particles were mixed with polyphenols extract, collagen type I and pectin from citrus peel (from Sigma-Aldrich) in order to form a injectable paste. Release study, antioxidant assay, HPLC analysis of extract, in vitro and in vivo test were performed. title: AAI-1: Agent Attestation Interface — Per-Action Cryptographic Attestation Protocol for Autonomous AI Agents: The First Published Per-Action Attestation Specification for Agentic Systems, with Documented Incident Analysis and Multi-Framework Regulatory Mapping
abstract: This specification defines AAI-1, the Agent Attestation Interface — the first published per-action cryptographic attestation protocol for autonomous AI agents. AAI-1 establishes a normative claim vocabulary, composition algebra, and conformance framework enabling cryptographically verifiable evidence of agent behavior at the granularity required for governance, incident response, regulatory enforcement, and forensic reconstruction.The specification addresses a substrate gap that no existing standard fills. The IETF Workload Identity Working Group has produced four agent identity drafts (Messous, Huang/expired, Jiang, PTV) addressing identity and authorization but not per-action behavioral attestation. The Model Context Protocol's authorization framework (RFC 9728) addresses tool access but not action-level governance. The OpenID AuthZEN Working Group's draft addresses access decisions but not the cryptographic record those decisions require. AAI-1 occupies the per-action attestation layer that current standards leave unspecified.AAI-1 defines forty claims across seven families: Identity Binding (Family 1), Capability Declaration (Family 2), Tool Invocation Binding (Family 3, novel), State Mutation Receipt (Family 4, novel), Cross-Principal Handoff (Family 5, novel), Channel and Session (Family 6), and Composition Context (Family 7, novel). Four claim families are introduced for the first time in this specification, addressing failure modes documented in the Part 3 case record that no current standard addresses at the substrate level.The composition algebra extension specifies how AAI-1 receipts compose across sequential, parallel, conditional, and recursive agent operations. The Model Context Protocol governance extension specifies how AAI-1 mitigates the documented MCP CVE patterns. Six sector conformance profiles (autonomous trading, AML investigation, insurance claims, customer onboarding, developer tool agents, medical decision support) provide procurement-ready compliance language calibrated to specific regulatory frameworks. Four operational methodologies (Agent Inventory, Incident Classification, Portable Agent Specification v2, Forensic Reconstruction) provide deployment-ready governance procedures. Four conformance tiers (AAI-C0 Reference through AAI-C3 Sovereign with TEE anchoring and multi-verifier redundancy) support adoption from research environments through national-security-adjacent deployments.Multi-framework regulatory mapping addresses eight articles of the EU AI Act, seven articles of DORA, the U.S. NDAA Sections 1512-1513, OMB Memoranda M-25-21 and M-25-22, Colorado Senate Bill 24-205, MiFID II RTS 6, ECB Guide to Internal Models, and FDA SaMD guidance. The Lanthorn reference implementation demonstrates browser-based AAI-1 receipt emission with full CDDL schema validation and reference test vectors covering all seven claim families.Part 2 documents the structural context within which the specification is required: the social media era as governance precedent, the agent economy as successor to the attention economy, the categorical differences between agent risk and general AI risk, the theoretical case for user control as governance infrastructure, the current trust infrastructure landscape, and the temporal window within which governance infrastructure adoption is most consequential.Part 3 documents eight specific incidents from July 2025 through April 2026, analyzed against the specification at the claim-number level. The incidents span four failure modes: human-attacker-exploits-agent (the Mexican government breach exposing 195 million identities through Claude Code and GPT-4.1; the GTG-1002 China-linked espionage campaign), agent-exploits-its-own-environment (the Alibaba ROME reverse-SSH-tunnel and unauthorized cryptocurrency mining incident), agent-violates-explicit-human-instruction (the Replit production database deletion during an active code freeze), and agent-exhibits-reward-hacking-drift (the IBM autonomous customer-service agent refund-policy violation). Each incident is mapped to specific AAI-1 claims and categorized by outcome (prevention, detection during attack, or post-hoc evidence). Part 3 additionally documents the policy-level articulation of the governance gap by AI Governance and Safety Canada in testimony before the Canadian House of Commons Standing Committee on Industry and Technology, the current-state alignment of Canadian regulatory frameworks with the testimony recommendations, and the architectural composition relationship between AAI-1's attestation layer and a complementary enforcement layer anticipated as a subsequent Auburn Patent Family clause.This document is Clause AI-10 of the Auburn Patent Family. It composes with MAI-1 (Clause AI-5, Model Attestation Interface), CRSA-1 (Clause AI-9, Compositional Runtime Safety Attestation), and AGS-1 (Clause AI-11, Auburn Governance Stack Architecture). The Autonomous AI Agents in Regulated Financial Services framework (DOI 10.6084/m9.figshare.31516171) is operationally implementable through AAI-1 conformance; this specification provides the per-action attestation substrate that the financial-services framework's compliance profiles require.The specification is published in three parts. Part 1 is the normative specification (Sections 1-19 and Appendices A-E), defining what AAI-1 is and how conformance is evaluated. Part 2 is informational context (Sections P2.1-P2.7), documenting why AAI-1 is required at the structural level. Part 3 is informational case analysis (Sections P3.1-P3.12), documenting what AAI-1 would have done against the public incident record. The three parts compose into a complete document. Each part is self-contained at its own scope.

title: Learning World Models for Unconstrained Goal Navigation
abstract: Learning world models offers a promising avenue for goal-conditioned reinforcement learning with sparse rewards. By allowing agents to plan actions or exploratory goals without direct interaction with the environment, world models enhance exploration efficiency. The quality of a world model hinges on the richness of data stored in the agent's replay buffer, with expectations of reasonable generalization across the state space surrounding recorded trajectories. However, challenges arise in generalizing learned world models to state transitions backward along recorded trajectories or between states across different trajectories, hindering their ability to accurately model real-world dynamics. To address these challenges, we introduce a novel goal-directed exploration algorithm, MUN (short for "World Models for Unconstrained Goal Navigation"). This algorithm is capable of modeling state transitions between arbitrary subgoal states in the replay buffer, thereby facilitating the learning of policies to navigate between any "key" states. Experimental results demonstrate that MUN strengthens the reliability of world models and significantly improves the policy's capacity to generalize across new goal settings.

title: Doctrinops evaluation harness: spec-driven compilation, hierarchical routing, and coverage-refusal benchmarks for a deployed MCP assistant
abstract: Evaluation harness for the paper 'Spec-Driven Compilation, Hierarchical Routing, and Coverage Refusal for a Deployed Multi-Tool MCP Assistant in Fire & Rescue Services' (NGEN-AI 2026, Springer CCIS). It reuses the production code paths of Doctrinops, a deployed assistant for French fire and rescue services built on the Model Context Protocol. Contents: (i) C1, callable-tool counts with and without a six-pass OpenAPI sanitation pipeline and leave-one-out attribution; (ii) C2, a 623-query expert-authored routing set, model results, 462 retained revision-replay predictions, a TF-IDF baseline, and exact paired McNemar statistics; (iii) C3, 67 geographic coverage probes, aggregate coverage-refusal results, and inter-family judge-agreement results. The public archive excludes raw operational answers and textual judge outputs, while retaining the scripts, benchmark inputs, labels, and aggregate results needed to audit the reported measurements. See eval/README.md for reproduction instructions.

title: A Formal Architecture for Governed Enterprise AI Agents: Forms, Lifecycle, and Accountability
abstract: Enterprise AI agents are increasingly deployed across workflows, platforms, and organizational boundaries as autonomous decision-makers with real operational consequences. Yet no formal architecture exists that simultaneously addresses what kinds of agents exist in enterprise settings, how they transition through operational states, who may authorize them to act, and how their actions are traced for accountability. Existing frameworks address these questions piecemeal: cognitive architectures model reasoning without governance; orchestration frameworks implement coordination without formal authority models; digital-twin formalisms cover lifecycle without delegation semantics. This paper presents a formal architecture for governed enterprise AI agents organized around four interlocking contributions. (1) An identity-anchored taxonomy classifies enterprise agents as Independent, Delegated, Asset-Bound, and Embedded agents, each with a defined authority source, identity anchor, lifecycle coupling, audit evidence type, and characteristic governance failure mode. Task labels such as analytical agent, coding agent, customer-service agent, or compliance-review agent are treated as deployment scenarios rather than primitive agent forms. (2) A three-layer governance architecture structures each agent across a cognitive layer (L_C), a platform layer (L_P), and an organizational layer (L_O), with explicit inter-layer accountability flows. (3) A lifecycle finite-state machine (FSM) with seven states — Design, Approval, Deployment, Operation, Adaptation, Suspension, and Retirement — formalizes the governance obligations and permissible transitions at each phase, including mandatory human-in-the-loop checkpoints at Approval and Suspension. (4) A delegation relation δ maps human principals to agent authority scopes using form-conditioned source authority and a policy cap, so that multiple partial grants cannot aggregate into unauthorized privilege escalation and delegation chains remain bounded. The architecture is grounded by an accountability matrix that cross-references agent form against governance instrument, audit evidence, escalation path, and compliance artifact. Four enterprise deployment scenarios — independent customer/IT service, delegated data governance, asset-bound operations, and embedded software engineering assistance — instantiate the architecture and demonstrate its practical discriminating power across the four identity-anchored forms and multiple task modes. title: Agentic Witnessing: Pragmatic and Scalable TEE-Enabled Privacy-Preserving Auditing
abstract: Auditing the semantic properties of proprietary data creates a fundamental tension: verification requires transparent access, while proprietary rights demand confidentiality. While Zero-Knowledge Proofs (ZKPs) ensure privacy, they are typically limited to precise algebraic constraints and are ill-suited for verifying qualitative, unstructured properties, such as the logic within a codebase. We propose {\em Agentic Witnessing}, a framework that moves verification from attested execution to {\em attested reasoning}. The system is composed of three agents: a Verifier (who wants to check properties of a dataset), a Prover (who owns the dataset) and an Auditor (that inspects the dataset). The Verifier is allowed to ask a limited number of simple binary true/false questions to the auditor. By isolating an LLM-based Auditor within a Trusted Execution Environment (TEE), the system enables the Verifier to query a Prover's private data via simple Boolean queries, without exposing the raw dataset. The Auditor uses the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to dynamically inspect the target dataset, producing a yes/no verdict accompanied by a cryptographic transcript: a signed hash chain binding the reasoning trace to both the original dataset and the TEE's hardware root of trust. We demonstrate this architecture by automating the artifact evaluation process for 21 peer-reviewed computer science papers with released codebases on GitHub (e.g. Does the codebase implement the system described in the paper?). We verified five high-level properties of these codebases described in the corresponding publications, treating the source code as private. Our results show that TEE-enabled agentic auditing provides a mechanism for privacy-preserving oversight, effectively decoupling qualitative verification from the need for data disclosure.

title: Capability-Aligned Hierarchical Learning for Tool-Augmented LLMs
abstract: Tool learning enables LLMs to invoke external tools to accomplish tasks. Prior studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of a hierarchical structure: a high-level policy handles global planning and decomposes tasks into manageable sub-tasks, and a low-level policy focuses on invoking tools to solve these sub-tasks. However, these works typically optimize the high-level and low-level policies separately, leading to planner-executor misalignment and limiting LLM performance on tool-use tasks. In this paper, we propose a method called Capability-Aligned Hierarchical Learning (CAHL), which leverages RLVR to jointly optimize both policies, enabling better alignment between the high-level planner and the low-level executor. Experiments on constrained tool-use benchmarks (API-Bank and BFCL) and an open-ended environment (Bamboogle) demonstrate the effectiveness of CAHL.

title: Chromacity Ltd.: Tuning capabilities of the Chromacity Near-IR Optical Parametric Oscillator (OPO)

Tunability and high average power enables a broad range of spectroscopic and sensing applications. Generating broadband coherent light at a high repetition rate (100 MHz) is key to setups that are detecting a wide range of solids, liquids and gases for materials characterisation, stand-off and explosive detection. A key application for the Chromacity Near-IR OPO is Fourier-transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy. title: The Scope and Use of the Attorney-Client Privilege in the U.S. and Its Applicability to Communications at Home and Abroad
abstract: ALTHOUGH the attorney-client privilege has been described as, one of the most revered of common law privileges, (1) recent developments have challenged the scope and use of the privilege, particularly concerning government investigations of corporate clients. In a recent survey by the National Association of Criminal Defense Lawyers, 87 percent of lawyers surveyed reported that they had experienced recent challenges to the attorney-client privilege. (2) Additionally, 85 percent reported that the Department of Justice and Securities and Exchange Commission frequently require waiver discussions when negotiating settlements. (3) Reviewing the characteristics of the privilege in the United States will aid clients and practitioners in ensuring that their communications remain as securely shielded by the attorney-client privilege as possible. What the Privilege Is The attorney-client privilege the oldest confidential communications privilege known to the common law. (4) Though each U.S. jurisdiction retains its own particular privilege test, often codified by statute, most jurisdictions require the same four elements for establishing privilege. There must be (1) a communication (2) between counsel and client (3) made confidentially (4) for the purpose of obtaining or rendering legal advice. (5) Though most jurisdictions have extended the privilege to include a client's confidential communications with a subordinate or outside agent assisting an attorney, the communication must always be confidential and made for the purpose of obtaining or rendering legal advice. (6) The privilege protects these communications to encourage frank discussions between a client and an attorney and to ensure that an attorney is not hindered in providing legal advice and services to a client. (7) The attorney-client privilege rests with the client and survives an individual client's death. (8) What It Is Not Jurisdictions also are similar in what they do not protect under the attorney-client privilege. First, the privilege does not protect facts, including those imbedded within otherwise privileged communications. (9) Even facts concerning the attorney-client relationship itself, such as a client's identity, whether such a relationship exists, when an attorney was retained, or the terms of the attorney's engagement, usually are not privileged. (10) Additionally, the attorney-client privilege applicable only to information sought for the purpose of obtaining legal advice and to communications involving an attorney acting as a legal advisor. (11) Therefore, business advice rendered by an attorney not privileged. (12) As a practical matter, documents containing both privileged communications and facts or business advice likely are discoverable, but may be redacted before production. The attorney-client privilege also does not protect information that counsel obtained from third parties during the course of representation. (13) Therefore, communications from counsel to the client disclosing information from third parties would not be protected because the underlying communication between counsel and the third party not protected. (14) Counsel's notes and impressions of third party conversations may be protected, however, as attorney work product. Choice of Law Because jurisdictions each have their own particular attorney-client privilege laws, choice or conflict of law issues can arise. Federal courts sitting in diversity jurisdiction apply state law concerning the attorney-client privilege. (15) A court determines which state's privilege laws apply by analyzing the forum state's choice or conflict of law principles. (16) States generally look to the state with the greatest interest or most significant relationship to the case generally, or to the privilege issue specifically. (17) Among the factors analyzed are: choice of law agreements, the principal locations of the parties involved, the location of the disputed occurrence, the location of the communication, where discovery occurring, and where any waiver alleged to have occurred. …

title: Energy poverty in China's energy transition era: capabilities, vulnerabilities and structural local dynamics
abstract: Energy poverty is increasingly recognized as a multidimensional condition that exceeds inadequate access to energy or the inability to afford fuel. It is constituted through the uneven capacity of households to utilize energy sources, infrastructures, technologies, and social arrangements and turn them into reliable, affordable, and meaningful energy services. This problem is especially acute in rural northern China, where long winters, dispersed settlements, ageing populations, infrastructural unevenness, and the ongoing clean energy transition reshape both the experience and governance of domestic energy poverty. Existing research on energy poverty in China has generated important insights through quantitative measurement, index construction, and panel-data analysis. However, this literature remains shaped by two closely related limitations. Definitional approaches have tended to privilege dimensions of deprivation that are visible, measurable, and administratively legible, particularly access, affordability, and consumption. Such approaches are less able to capture the situated meanings of energy poverty in rural China, where hardship may be concealed through coping practices, normalized discomfort, seasonal adjustment, and the downward recalibration of expectations. Methodologically, the dominance of historical quantitative datasets has limited understanding of how energy poverty is lived, why it emerges in particular households and villages, and how it is reproduced through social relations, housing conditions, infrastructures, local governance, and policy implementation. A further gap concerns the clean energy transition itself: existing evaluations have focused largely on adoption rates, aggregate welfare effects, or technological outcomes, rather than on the implementation processes and service-delivery arrangements through which some households become included while others are left behind. This thesis addresses these gaps by developing a contextualized, mixed-methods account of how energy poverty is experienced, produced, and reproduced through rural clean-heating transition in northern China. The thesis develops a mixed-methods analysis based on two rounds of fieldwork conducted between 2023 and 2024 across 20 rural villages in Shanxi, Hebei, and Inner Mongolia. It combines qualitative interviews, field observations, documentary analysis, thematic analysis, and an evolutionary game theory–agent-based model. Qualitative evidence is used not only to interpret lived experiences and multi-scalar drivers of energy poverty, but also to inform the quantitative modelling of stakeholder payoffs, behavioural dynamics, and policy scenarios. In doing so, the thesis links situated empirical accounts of domestic energy hardship with a forward-looking assessment of clean-heating implementation under real-world institutional constraints. The first empirical study advances a capability-based understanding of energy poverty by incorporating conversion burdens and coping strategies into the capability framework. It shows that energy poverty in rural northern China is strongly seasonal, with winter hardship producing more severe capability deprivation than summer heat. Households reliant on traditional fuels experience the most acute burdens because obtaining, transporting, storing, and converting fuels into usable heat requires substantial labor, time, money, bodily effort, and practical knowledge. These burdens do not merely accompany energy poverty but also erode the very capabilities needed to secure energy services. The chapter therefore identifies a conditional Energy Poverty–Capability Deprivation loop, in which traditional-fuel households preserve basic functionings through conversion efforts and coping strategies that simultaneously constrain health, mobility, comfort, autonomy, care, and social participation. This finding extends capability-informed energy poverty scholarship by showing that energy poverty is not only a failure to achieve adequate energy services, but also a process through which securing and coping with those services can deplete household capability sets. The second empirical study examines how social, cultural, economic, material, geographical, and regulatory factors interact to shape energy poverty. It demonstrates that rural energy poverty cannot be reduced to household income alone. Agricultural livelihoods, unstable or limited cash income, ageing and shrinking households, substandard and thermally inefficient housing, partial heating practices, village location, infrastructural delays, and uneven access to modern energy services together produce differentiated vulnerability. Social relations and family arrangements can mitigate hardship through support, care, and resource sharing, yet they may also deepen vulnerability where older people live alone, support networks are thin, or household labor is insufficient. The chapter further shows that energy transition can generate unintended forms of exclusion, including temporal service gaps, higher energy expenditure, and uneven access to infrastructure. These findings foreground energy poverty as a relational and context-specific condition produced through the interaction of household circumstances, village environments, and transition processes. The third empirical study examines whether current clean-heating transition arrangements can alleviate energy poverty over time. Focusing on Yangcheng County in Shanxi Province, it couples evolutionary game theory with agent-based modelling to represent interactions among households, village committees, and heating enterprises across district heating, coal-to-gas, and coal-to-electricity pathways. The simulations compare an idealized implementation setting with a constrained setting parameterized from observed zoning, contracting, and tariff under-recovery. The results show that, as subsidies decline, policy targets and realized access increasingly diverge. In the constrained scenario, up to 40% of households fall outside effective access over a 20-year period, with energy-poor households facing the greatest risk of exclusion. This exclusion is driven by a self-reinforcing service lock-out mechanism: weak cost recovery leads providers to ration maintenance, which reduces household willingness to pay, further undermines enterprise finances, and ultimately strands marginal villages. The analysis shows that subsidy expansion alone cannot remove this inclusion ceiling because the underlying problem lies in the design of the clean-heating service delivery regime. This discussion synthesizes the three empirical studies by demonstrating how, collectively, they address the six research questions posed at the outset of this thesis. It begins by clarifying the research's contributions to existing scholarship in relation to the gaps identified in the literature review. Taken together, the three empirical studies make a more specific contribution to energy poverty scholarship by shifting the analytical focus from energy access, affordability, and technology adoption towards the service relationships through which deprivation is produced, managed, and prolonged. First, the thesis extends capability-based energy poverty analysis by showing that deprivation is not confined to the absence of adequate energy services. It can also arise from the burdensome work required to obtain fuels, convert them into usable services, and cope with partial or unreliable provision. This reframes coping strategies not simply as household resilience, but as a capability-consuming practice that may preserve basic functionings while narrowing wider possibilities for health, comfort, mobility, care, autonomy, and social participation. Second, the thesis advances a relational account of rural energy poverty by demonstrating how household vulnerability is constituted through village infrastructures, kinship arrangements, housing conditions, local governance capacity, and energy-service markets. Energy poverty therefore appears not as an isolated household deficit, but as a structurally embedded condition unevenly distributed through socio-material and institutional arrangements. Third, by linking qualitative lived-experience evidence with evolutionary game and agent-based modelling, the thesis shows how present forms of hardship may become future patterns of exclusion under the clean-heating transition. This methodological integration enables the thesis to move beyond retrospective explanation and to identify the service-delivery mechanisms through which policy ambition can translate into long-term lock-out for energy-poor households. The thesis also develops three cross-cutting themes that emerge across the empirical chapters: (1) energy poverty under hybrid energy systems—spatial–temporal dynamics and household vulnerability; (2) from household vulnerability to market retrenchment—demographic decline and energy poverty entrapment in clean energy transitions; and (3) direct clean energy transition toward energy justice in the absence of targeted policy intervention to address energy poverty. The thesis concludes that alleviating energy poverty in rural northern China requires more than fuel substitution, infrastructure expansion, or household subsidies. Durable alleviation depends on strengthening the institutional and collective conditions through which households can secure adequate energy services without eroding their own capabilities. Three policy directions follow. First, targeted subsidies should combine seasonal energy-cost support with housing-efficiency assessment, retrofit assistance, and minimum consumption support. Second, community-based collective infrastructures, including warm spaces, emergency heating support, coordinated fuel access, village funds, energy advice, and peer learning, should be developed to reduce household-level conversion burdens.
